subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 7, mathematicians! In this unit you will explore the fascinating world of fractions. A fraction is simply a way of describing parts of a whole or parts of a group. You already meet fractions every single day without always noticing. When Amina shares an anjero equally between her three brothers, when Yusuf drinks half of his camel-milk cup, or when Halima measures three-quarters of a cup of flour to make sambusa dough at home in Hargeisa, they are all thinking in fractions.

This unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, try every worked example yourself on paper, and only move on when you feel ready. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you extra practice, explain a step in a fresh way, or check your answers. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky.

Why do fractions matter so much? Because the world is not always made of whole numbers. A trader at the Bakaara market rarely sells exactly one whole sack; he sells half a sack, or a quarter. A recipe rarely calls for a whole cup; it calls for two-thirds. A school day splits into parts, and money set aside for charity is worked out as a fraction of what a family earns. When you become confident with fractions, you gain a tool you will use for the rest of your life – and you build the foundation you need for decimals, percentages and ratio in the years ahead.

As you work, keep a pencil and some paper beside you, and if you can, some real objects to divide – a piece of paper to fold, some dates to share, or a drawing of a chocolate bar to shade. Mathematics is not a subject you can learn only by reading; you must do it. Fold the paper, shade the parts, and say the fractions out loud. If you get something wrong, that is not a failure – it is simply a signpost showing you exactly what to practise next.

outcomes: Recognise and write fractions as equal parts of a whole or a group.
Represent fractions with different models: area models, number lines and set models.
Read and write fractions in words and symbols (for example, 3/4 and ‘three-quarters’).
Compare and order fractions with the same denominator.
Compare and order fractions with the same numerator.
Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator.
Relate a fraction to division (recognise that a/b means the same as a ÷ b, for example 3/4 means 3 shared equally among 4).
Position mixed numbers accurately on a number line that extends beyond 1.

concepts.title: What a Fraction Really Means
concepts.explanation: A fraction represents equal parts of a whole. The most important word in that sentence is equal — every part must be exactly the same size. If Farah divides a chocolate bar into 4 pieces but makes one piece huge and the others tiny, those are not quarters, because they are not equal. Fair sharing always means equal parts. Imagine we divide a chocolate bar into 4 equal pieces and take 3 of them. We have taken 3/4 (three-quarters) of the bar. Picture the bar as four equal squares in a row, with three of them shaded… There is another powerful way to think about a fraction: as a division that has not been worked out yet. The fraction 1/4 means exactly the same as 1 ÷ 4 — one whole shared equally among 4 people. If 3 flatbreads are shared equally between 4 people, each person's share is 3 ÷ 4, which is exactly the same amount as the fraction 3/4. In general, any fraction a/b means the same as a ÷ b: the numerator is the amount being shared, and the denominator is the number of equal shares it is split into. This is exactly why the fraction bar looks so much like a division sign — it is doing the very same job.
concepts.example: Every fraction is built from two numbers, one written above the other with a line between them: the numerator (top) tells you how many parts you have, and the denominator (bottom) tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into.

concepts.title: Reading and Writing Fractions
concepts.explanation: Fractions can be written in symbols (like 3/4) or in words (like three-quarters). You need to move easily between the two. Here are the common fractions you will meet most often: 1/2 one-half, 1/3 one-third, 1/4 one-quarter, 1/5 one-fifth, 1/8 one-eighth, 1/10 one-tenth. So 5/8 is read ‘five-eighths’: the denominator 8 gives ‘eighth’, and because the numerator 5 is more than one we add an ‘s’. In the same way, 7/9 is ‘seven-ninths’ and 2/5 is ‘two-fifths’. Practise saying them aloud — hearing the words helps the meaning stick.

concepts.title: Three Ways to Show a Fraction
concepts.explanation:
One fraction can be pictured in several different ways. Being able to move between these pictures is a sign that you truly understand what the fraction means. There are three models you should master.

An area model shows a fraction as part of a shape. The shape is divided into equal parts, and some parts are shaded. For example, a circle divided into 4 equal parts with 1 part shaded shows 1/4. A rectangle divided into 3 equal parts with 2 shaded shows 2/3. Area models are the pictures most people imagine first when they think of a fraction – like slices of a round anjero or squares of a chocolate bar.

A length model shows a fraction on a number line. The distance from 0 to 1 is divided into equal steps, one step for each part named by the denominator. For example, on a number line from 0 to 1 divided into 5 equal parts, the third mark stands for 3/5. Number lines are powerful because they show clearly that a fraction is a number with its own place, sitting somewhere between 0 and 1.

A set model shows a fraction as part of a group of objects. For example, if you have 8 marbles and 3 of them are red, then 3/8 of the marbles are red. If Khadija has 10 dates and gives away 7, she has given away 7/10 of them. In a set model the denominator counts how many objects are in the whole group, and the numerator counts how many you are choosing.
concepts.example: Here is something important that often surprises people: equal parts must be the same size, but they do not have to be the same shape. A rectangle can be cut into fourths as four equal small rectangles, or as four equal triangles, or even four equal L-shapes. As long as each part covers exactly 1/4 of the total area, it is a true quarter. What matters is equal area, not identical shape.

concepts.title: Comparing Fractions with the Same Denominator
concepts.explanation:
When two fractions have the same denominator, the pieces are all the same size, so comparing them is easy: the fraction with the larger numerator is larger. You are simply counting how many equal pieces each one has.

For example, 3/5 is greater than 2/5 because 3 pieces is more than 2 pieces of the very same size (3 > 2). In the same way, 7/8 is greater than 3/8 because 7 > 3, and 1/4 is less than 3/4 because 1 < 3. We record these comparisons using three symbols: > (greater than), < (less than) and = (equal to).
concepts.example: So we can write 3/5 > 2/5 or 1/4 < 3/4. A helpful trick many learners use: the open, hungry mouth of the > or < symbol always points towards the bigger fraction, like a crocodile that wants the larger meal. When the denominators match, just line up the numerators and let the crocodile face the larger one.

concepts.title: Comparing Fractions with the Same Numerator
concepts.explanation:
Comparing fractions with the same numerator works the opposite way, and this often surprises learners. When the numerators are the same, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger.

Why? Because the denominator tells you how many pieces the whole is cut into. When you cut a whole into more pieces, each piece becomes smaller. So thirds are bigger than fifths, and fifths are bigger than tenths. If you have one piece each way, one third is a bigger bite than one fifth.

For example, 2/3 is greater than 2/5, because thirds are larger than fifths (imagine cutting the same anjero into 3 pieces versus 5 pieces – the 3-piece cuts are bigger). In the same way, 3/4 is greater than 3/8, because quarters are larger than eighths, and 1/2 is greater than 1/10, because halves are far larger than tenths. So we write 2/3 > 2/5 and 3/4 > 3/8.
concepts.example: This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, so hold onto it: when the numerator stays the same, a bigger denominator makes a smaller fraction. Many people get this backwards because they see the big number 5 in 1/5 and assume it must be large. But 1/5 is smaller than 1/3. Always think about the size of the pieces, not just the size of the digits.

concepts.title: Ordering Fractions and Using a Number Line
concepts.explanation: To order fractions means to line them up, usually from smallest to largest. A number line is a wonderful tool for this. To place a fraction on a number line from 0 to 1, you divide the space between 0 and 1 into equal parts based on the denominator, then count along from 0 the number of parts given by the numerator. For example, to place 3/4 on a number line: divide the space from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts, then count 3 parts from 0. Your mark lands three-quarters of the way along, close to 1. When you have several fractions to order, place each one on the line and then read them from left to right – that gives you smallest to largest automatically. So far every fraction has fitted between 0 and 1, but a number line does not stop at 1 – it carries on past 1, 2, 3 and beyond. Past the whole number 1 comes a mixed number such as 1 1/4: a whole one, plus a further quarter of the way towards 2. To place a mixed number like 2 3/4 on a number line, first count along to its whole-number part (2), then divide the space from that point up to the next whole number (3) into the number of equal parts shown by the denominator (4), and count along the number of parts shown by the numerator (3). So 2 3/4 lands three-quarters of the way between the marks for 2 and 3.
concepts.example: If all your fractions share the same denominator, you do not even need to draw the line carefully; just order the numerators. To order 1/4, 3/4 and 2/4, look at the numerators 1, 3, 2 and put them in order: 1, 2, 3. So the fractions in order are 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. If instead the fractions share the same numerator, order them by denominator from largest denominator (smallest fraction) to smallest denominator (largest fraction): 1/10, 1/5, 1/2.

methods.title: How to compare two fractions
steps: Check whether the denominators are the same or the numerators are the same.
Same denominators: the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
Same numerators: the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction.
Write the correct symbol: >, < or =.

methods.title: How to find an equivalent fraction
steps: Choose a number to multiply (or divide) by.
Multiply (or divide) the numerator by that number.
Do exactly the same to the denominator.
Check: the new fraction should cover the same amount.

methods.title: How to add or subtract fractions with the same denominator
steps: Check the denominators are the same.
Add or subtract the numerators.
Keep the denominator unchanged.
Simplify the answer if the top and bottom share a common factor.

methods.title: How to find a fraction of an amount
methods.example: Farah has 15 dates and gives 2/5 of them to her little brother. How many dates does she give away?
steps: Divide the amount by the denominator to find one part.
Multiply that part by the numerator (for a unit fraction, the numerator is 1).
The result is the fraction of the amount.

methods.title: Find equivalent fractions
steps: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number each time.
×3 gives 6/9.
×4 gives 8/12.

methods.title: Add fractions
steps: The denominators match, so add the numerators and keep the denominator: 2 + 3 = 5, so the answer is 5/6.
(5/6 cannot be simplified, so we leave it as it is.)
Check the denominators still match your original fractions, and that your answer cannot be simplified further.

workedExamples.title: Name the fraction
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangle is divided into 6 equal parts and 5 of them are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
workedExamples.solution: The whole is split into 6 equal parts, so the denominator is 6. Five parts are shaded, so the numerator is 5. The shaded fraction is 5/6, read ‘five-sixths’.

workedExamples.title: Write a fraction in words
workedExamples.solution: The denominator 5 gives ‘fifth’. The numerator 4 is more than one, so we add an ‘s’ to make it plural. The answer is four-fifths.

workedExamples.title: Compare (same denominator)
workedExamples.solution: The denominators are equal, so compare the numerators. Since 5 > 3, we have 5/8 > 3/8. The crocodile mouth opens towards 5/8.

workedExamples.title: Compare (same numerator)
workedExamples.solution: The numerators are equal, so compare the denominators. A smaller denominator makes bigger pieces, and 3 < 5, so thirds are bigger than fifths. Therefore 2/3 > 2/5.

workedExamples.title: Find equivalent fractions
workedExamples.solution: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number each time. ×2 gives (2×2)/(3×2) = 4/6. ×3 gives 6/9. ×4 gives 8/12. So three equivalent fractions are 4/6, 6/9 and 8/12.

workedExamples.title: Add fractions
workedExamples.solution: The denominators match, so add the numerators and keep the denominator: 2 + 3 = 5, so the answer is 5/6. (5/6 cannot be simplified, so we leave it as it is.)

workedExamples.title: Subtract and simplify
workedExamples.solution: Subtract the numerators, keep the denominator: 7 − 3 = 4, giving 4/8. Now simplify: divide top and bottom by 4 to get 1/2. So 7/8 − 3/8 = 4/8 = 1/2.

workedExamples.title: Fraction of an amount
workedExamples.prompt: A shirt costs 24 shillings. There is a 1/3 discount. How much is the discount, and what is the sale price?
workedExamples.solution: The discount is 1/3 of 24, which is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 shillings. The sale price is 24 − 8 = 16 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Order three fractions
workedExamples.prompt: Put 1/2, 1/5 and 1/10 in order from smallest to largest.
workedExamples.solution: The numerators are all 1, so the fraction with the largest denominator is the smallest. The denominators are 2, 5 and 10. Largest denominator first (smallest fraction): 1/10, 1/5, 1/2.

workedExamples.title: Two-step fraction of an amount
workedExamples.prompt: Farah has 15 dates and gives 2/5 of them to her little brother. How many dates does she give away?
workedExamples.solution: Divide by the denominator to find one fifth: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 dates. Then multiply by the numerator to find two fifths: 3 × 2 = 6 dates. So Farah gives away 6 dates and keeps 9.

workedExamples.title: Find: several parts
workedExamples.prompt: Find: a) 1/4 of 20 b) 1/3 of 12 c) 1/2 of 3/4 cup.

activities.title: The Paper-Folding Fraction Kit
activities.materials: several sheets of paper, a pencil, and coloured pencils if you have them.
steps: Fold one sheet in half and open it. Shade one part. You have made 1/2.
Fold another sheet in half, then in half again. Open it: four equal parts, or quarters. Shade three to show 3/4.
Fold a third sheet into eighths. Shade parts to show 5/8.
Line up your halves, quarters and eighths. Can you see that 2/4 covers the same as 1/2, and 4/8 does too? You have discovered equivalent fractions.
Keep your folded sheets – they are a fraction wall you can use all through this unit.

activities.title: Fair Sharing (Set Models)
activities.materials: a small pile of dates, stones or bottle caps (about 12).
steps: Count out 12 dates. Share them equally between 3 people. What fraction does each person get? (1/3, and 1/3 of 12 = 4 dates.)
Now share the same 12 between 4 people. What fraction each? (1/4, and that is 3 dates each.)
Colour or set aside 3 of the 12 dates. What fraction have you set aside? (3/12, which simplifies to 1/4.)
Ask a family member to name a fraction of the pile, and you set aside that many.

activities.title: The Fraction Comparison Card Game
activities.materials: paper cards, each with a simple fraction written on it (for example 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 2/5, 3/8, 5/6).
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down.
Each player turns over one card.
Decide which fraction is greater. If the denominators match, compare numerators; if the numerators match, remember that the smaller denominator wins.
Draw a crocodile mouth (> or <) pointing at the greater fraction. The greater card wins the round.
This game trains you to compare fractions quickly and to explain your reasoning out loud.

activities.title: Build a Number Line
activities.materials: a long strip of paper, a ruler and a pencil.
steps: Draw a straight line and mark 0 at the left end and 1 at the right end.
Divide the space between 0 and 1 into 4 equal parts. Label the marks 1/4, 2/4, 3/4.
On a second line, divide 0 to 1 into 8 equal parts and label them in eighths.
Place the two lines one above the other. Which eighths line up with the quarters? (2/8 with 1/4, 4/8 with 2/4, 6/8 with 3/4.) You have found more equivalent fractions.

activities.title: Kitchen Fraction Investigation (Family Task)
activities.materials: a measuring cup and something safe to measure, such as rice, flour or water, with an adult helping.
steps: Measure out 1/2 a cup, then 1/4 of a cup. Pour the 1/4 into the 1/2 twice. What do you notice? (Two quarters fill one half: 2/4 = 1/2.)
A recipe needs 3/4 cup of flour. You have already added 1/4 cup. Measure how much more you need. (2/4 = 1/2 a cup more.)
Halve a recipe that asks for 3/4 cup of sugar. How much do you use? (1/2 of 3/4 = 3/8 cup.)
Talk about where else fractions appear in cooking.

activities.title: Design Your Own Fraction Story
steps: Write a short story problem that uses adding fractions with the same denominator.
Write another that uses subtracting fractions with the same denominator.
Write a third about finding a fraction of an amount of shillings.
Swap stories with a friend or family member and solve each other’s problems.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand fractions best? What was the trickiest part? Did folding paper help you see equivalent fractions? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: What a Fraction Means
rules.text: Numerator (top) = how many parts you have. Denominator (bottom) = how many equal parts the whole is split into. Example: 3/4 means 3 of 4 equal parts.

rules.title: Comparing Rule
rules.text: Same denominator: the bigger numerator is the bigger fraction. Same numerator: the smaller denominator is the bigger fraction. More pieces in the whole means each piece is smaller.

rules.title: Equivalent Fractions Rule
rules.text: Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8. They all cover the same amount.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Same denominator: add or subtract the numerators only. Keep the denominator the same. Never add the bottoms. Simplify the answer if you can.

terms: A number for equal parts of a whole or group
The top number – how many parts you have
The bottom number – how many equal parts in the whole
Different fractions worth the same amount
A fraction reduced by dividing top and bottom
A fraction with numerator 1, such as 1/4
A line from 0 to 1 split into equal steps
commonMistakes: Parts must be equal in area
Divide top and bottom by 4 to get 1/2

realProblems.prompt: A shirt normally costs 24 shillings. With a 1/3 discount, how much is the discount and what is the sale price?
realProblems.answer: 1/3 of 24 = 8 shillings discount; sale price 24 − 8 = 16 shillings.

realProblems.prompt: Zahra’s water jar was 4/5 full and Noor’s identical jar was 7/10 full. Whose jar had more water, and by how much? (Hint: 4/5 = 8/10.)
realProblems.answer: Zahra’s jar had more: 4/5 = 8/10 and 8/10 > 7/10, so 8/10 − 7/10 = 1/10 more.

A carpenter has a 2-metre plank and uses 3/4 of it. How much wood does he use, and how much is left?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3/4 of 2 m = 1.5 m used, so 0.5 m left.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A blue ribbon is 3/4 metre long and a red ribbon is 3/5 metre long. Which is longer, and how do you know using same-numerator reasoning?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The blue ribbon is longer: 3/4 > 3/5 because with the same numerator, quarters are bigger than fifths.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing Fractions with the Same Numerator.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Comparing fractions with the same numerator works the opposite way, and this often surprises learners. When the numerators are the same, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger. Why? Because the denominator tells you how many pieces the whole is cut into. When you cut a whole into more pieces, each piece becomes smaller. So thirds are bigger than fifths, and fifths are bigger than tenths. If you have one piece each way, one third is a bigger bite than one fifth.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Ordering Fractions and Using a Number Line.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
To order fractions means to line them up, usually from smallest to largest. A number line is a wonderful tool for this. To place a fraction on a number line from 0 to 1, you divide the space between 0 and 1 into equal parts based on the denominator, then count along from 0 the number of parts given by the numerator.

For example, to place 3/4 on a number line: divide the space from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts, then count 3 parts from 0. Your mark lands three-quarters of the way along, close to 1. When you have several fractions to order, place each one on the line and then read them from left to right – that gives you smallest to largest automatically.

questions.question: Which is greater, 4/9 or 7/9?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: The denominators are the same, so compare the numerators: 7 > 4, so 7/9 is greater.

questions.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Simplest form" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: 2/4 simplifies to 1/2, so they are equivalent.

questions.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/3?
questions.hint: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
questions.explanation: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 2/3 by 2 to get 4/6, so 2/3 and 4/6 are equivalent.

questions.question: Work out 3/8 + 2/8.
questions.hint: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
questions.explanation: The denominators match, so add the numerators: 3 + 2 = 5, keeping the denominator 8. The answer is 5/8.

questions.question: Which fraction is larger: 1/2 or 1/4?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: Halves are bigger than quarters, so 1/2 is larger than 1/4.

questions.question: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Yusuf eats 3 slices and gives 2 slices to his sister. What fraction of the pizza is left?
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Numerator" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: 3 slices eaten plus 2 given away is 5 out of 8 slices gone, so 8 − 5 = 3 slices remain, which is 3/8 of the pizza.

selfAssessment: I can recognise and write fractions as equal parts of a whole or a group.
I can represent fractions with different models: area models, number lines and set models.
I can read and write fractions in words and symbols (for example, 3/4 and ‘three-quarters’).
I can compare and order fractions with the same denominator.
I can compare and order fractions with the same numerator.
I can identify and generate equivalent fractions.
I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator.
